paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships becomes harder when unobserved variables influence several measured variables. Some existing approaches handle these hidden influences through overcomplete independent component analysis, but their optimization can be expensive and get trapped in local optima. This paper develops an alternative that uses higher-order cumulants, statistical quantities that describe distributional structure beyond ordinary covariance.

The starting point is a special mixing structure called One-Latent-Component. In this setting, the authors identify a closed-form solution and use cumulants to estimate the mixing matrix. They also introduce a testable condition for identifying latent variables and determining causal order. This turns a structural property of the data-generating process into a tool for causal discovery.

To handle multiple latent components, the method repeatedly removes shared components that it has already identified. The authors establish asymptotic correctness for the resulting algorithm and report experiments supporting its effectiveness. The result extends the special-case construction to a broader latent-variable structure; its correctness claim concerns the large-data limit within the analyzed setting.
icml-2023-causal-discovery-with-latent-c.tldr: Higher-order cumulants enable a causal discovery algorithm that identifies and removes latent components, with asymptotic correctness in the analyzed setting.

paragraphs: Many machine learning objectives have parameters that naturally divide into blocks. Updating these blocks in a fixed cycle can be useful, but understanding convergence is difficult when the objective is nonconvex and combines smooth and nonsmooth terms. This paper develops cyclic block coordinate methods with guarantees that describe progress after a finite amount of computation.

The analysis uses a gradient smoothness condition measured through a Mahalanobis norm. In the deterministic setting, the resulting guarantee matches the form of the guarantee for full-gradient descent, with the smoothness constant defined in this different geometry. For stochastic updates, recursive variance reduction lowers the cost per iteration while controlling noise in the gradient estimates.

The stochastic methods match the arithmetic complexity of current optimal stochastic full-gradient methods in the analyzed finite-sum and infinite-sum settings. Faster linear convergence additionally requires a Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition. Experiments on deep neural network training support the cyclic scheme's practical effectiveness, complementing the finite-computation theory for composite nonconvex objectives.
icml-2023-cyclic-block-coordinate-descen.tldr: Cyclic block updates with variance reduction achieve finite-computation convergence guarantees competitive with full-gradient methods for composite nonconvex optimization.

paragraphs: Learning in a multiplayer game raises two related questions: how well does each player perform while learning, and how quickly do the players approach equilibrium? Algorithms can have strong guarantees for one question without resolving the other. This paper introduces accelerated optimistic gradient, or AOG, to address both in smooth monotone games.

Under smooth, convex losses in an adversarial setting, AOG achieves the optimal O(√T) regret bound. In multiplayer smooth monotone games, its latest iterate approaches a Nash equilibrium at the optimal O(1/T) rate. The focus on the latest iterate matters because the guarantee describes the current strategies themselves. It improves on the O(1/√T) rate that is tight for several established algorithm families.

The authors also derive an O(log T) bound on each player's individual worst-case dynamic regret, compared with the previous O(√T) bound. These results connect accelerated equilibrium convergence with stronger guarantees during learning. Their scope is the stated smoothness, convexity, and monotonicity settings; the paper does not claim the same behavior for arbitrary games.
icml-2023-doubly-optimal-no-regret-learn.tldr: Accelerated optimistic gradient combines optimal adversarial regret with optimal last-iterate equilibrium convergence in smooth monotone games.

paragraphs: Physical simulations on meshes often require information to travel between distant parts of a system. A flat graph neural network can accomplish this through repeated message passing, but increasing the number of passes raises computational costs and can oversmooth representations. Multiscale networks offer another route, provided their coarser graphs preserve the geometry appropriately.

This paper introduces bi-stride pooling, which selects nodes from alternating breadth-first-search frontiers. The construction uses graph connectivity instead of requiring manually drawn coarse meshes or relying on spatial proximity. That distinction matters because points that are close in space can lie across a geometry boundary, where proximity-based connections would introduce incorrect edges.

The resulting BSMS-GNN uses fewer message-passing steps at each scale and interpolation-based pooling and unpooling without learned parameters. These choices reduce the computational requirements of multiscale processing. Experiments in representative physical simulation scenarios report substantial improvements in both accuracy and efficiency over existing methods, supporting the usefulness of connectivity-based coarsening for the evaluated mesh systems.
icml-2023-efficient-learning-of-mesh-bas.tldr: BSMS-GNN builds mesh hierarchies through graph-based bi-stride pooling, improving accuracy and computational efficiency in the reported physical simulations.

paragraphs: Regression trees offer interpretable predictions, but their ability to benefit from a very smooth target function can be limited. This paper introduces Extrapolated Random Tree for Regression, or ERTR, to adapt to arbitrary target smoothness while retaining tree interpretability. Its central idea is to combine estimates from trees constructed at different scaling ratios.

The authors first develop a homothetic random tree whose estimate converges to the target as its homothetic ratio approaches zero. ERTR then fits a linear regression to estimates obtained at several ratios and extrapolates to zero. The limiting behavior of this family of trees therefore becomes the basis for a prediction procedure.

For functions in general Hölder smoothness spaces, the authors establish optimal convergence rates. For higher-order smooth targets, a lower bound shows that ordinary random tree regression converges strictly more slowly. Real-data experiments report advantages over state-of-the-art tree algorithms, and using extrapolated trees within ensembles brings further promising improvements. Together, the results link the extrapolation step to both theoretical and empirical gains.
icml-2023-extrapolated-random-tree-for-r.tldr: ERTR extrapolates across scaled random-tree estimates to exploit higher-order smoothness while preserving interpretability.

paragraphs: A language model can contain useful abstract knowledge about how the world works while still making poor decisions in a particular environment. The problem is alignment between that knowledge and what actions actually accomplish. This paper studies functional grounding: connecting a model's decision-making behavior to feedback obtained through interaction with an environment.

The proposed approach, GLAM, uses a large language model as the agent's policy. Online reinforcement learning progressively updates that policy as the agent interacts and works toward goals. The learning process therefore gives the model opportunities to adapt its behavior using experience from the environment in which its decisions are applied.

The study uses an interactive textual environment with spatial and navigation tasks, examining FLAN-T5 variants that differ in size and architecture. It asks whether language models improve sample efficiency, how they affect different forms of generalization, and what online learning contributes. The abstract presents these as research questions rather than reporting specific answers, so the stated contribution is the grounding approach and its experimental investigation.
icml-2023-grounding-large-language-model.tldr: GLAM studies how online reinforcement learning can ground language-model policies through interaction in textual spatial and navigation tasks.

paragraphs: Sharing training data while protecting each person's label requires understanding what the released features reveal. Earlier label differential privacy analyses treated features as public and externally given. This paper studies a different setting in which the distribution of features depends on the private labels, bringing the relationship between features and labels into the privacy analysis.

Under this model, adding noise only to labels can provide an arbitrarily weak privacy guarantee. The problem is that privacy cannot be assessed solely through the label perturbation when features also carry relevant information. The authors additionally develop methods for estimating this privacy loss from data, making the issue something that can be investigated empirically.

Their proposed release mechanism replaces some training examples with synthetic data. They show a substantially better privacy-utility tradeoff when those synthetic examples meet a quantifiable realism condition. This condition is central to the result: the benefit depends on the quality of the synthetic distribution. Experiments support the theoretical analysis and its account of the privacy-accuracy relationship.
icml-2023-label-differential-privacy-and.tldr: When features depend on private labels, realistic synthetic replacements can improve the privacy-utility tradeoff over label noise alone.

paragraphs: Smooth functions change in a controlled way as their inputs move, a property relevant to learning stability and generalization. This paper studies how to learn functions that are globally smooth on a manifold, the lower-dimensional structure on which the data are modeled. The aim is to control variation across that structure through the learning objective.

The authors connect constrained learning with manifold regularization. Under typical conditions, they show that learning a Lipschitz-continuous function on a manifold is equivalent to a regularization problem with weights that change during learning. This equivalence provides a practical route from a global smoothness requirement to an objective that can be optimized.

The resulting algorithm uses a weighted Laplacian penalty and adapts its weights through stochastic gradient techniques. Under mild conditions, it also estimates the learned solution's Lipschitz constant, obtaining global smoothness as a byproduct. Real-data experiments illustrate advantages over existing alternatives. The theoretical contribution explains how adaptive regularization can enforce the desired smoothness within the stated conditions.
icml-2023-learning-globally-smooth-funct.tldr: Adaptive manifold regularization provides a practical way to learn globally smooth functions and estimate their Lipschitz constants under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Object detectors for resource-constrained systems must balance accuracy with computation and memory use. Knowledge distillation can help a small model learn from a larger one, but detection involves variable structured outputs and complicated internal modules. This makes transferring knowledge more challenging than in the classification setting where distillation is already well established.

The paper proposes teaching a lightweight detector progressively through a sequence of teacher models. This sequence helps the student gradually adapt before absorbing knowledge from a highly accurate, complex teacher. The strategy can be combined with existing detection distillation mechanisms, making the ordering of teachers an additional tool for improving the student.

The authors report successful transfer from Transformer-based teachers to convolution-based students. On MS COCO, ResNet-50 RetinaNet improves from 36.5% to 42.0% AP, while Mask R-CNN improves from 38.2% to 42.5% AP. These results demonstrate substantial gains in the reported configurations and support progressive teaching as a useful approach to bridging differences between teacher and student models.
icml-2023-learning-lightweight-object-de.tldr: A sequence of teacher detectors progressively improves lightweight students, including successful transfer from Transformer teachers to convolutional models.

paragraphs: In vertical federated learning, several parties hold different features for samples drawn from a shared ID space. They collaborate with a server to train a prediction model. Removing unimportant features can support generalization, efficiency, and explainability, but coordinating feature selection across the distributed system introduces communication costs.

LESS-VFL separates the coordination step from local feature selection. After a short pretraining stage, the server optimizes its portion of the global model to identify which outputs from the parties' models are relevant. It communicates that information to the parties, which then use it to select their own features without further communication during that local selection step.

The authors analytically establish that LESS-VFL removes spurious features from training. Their experiments also show that the method can retain high accuracy while removing such features at a fraction of the communication cost of other selection approaches. The contribution is a way to make local decisions informed by the global prediction task while reducing the communication needed for feature selection.
icml-2023-less-vfl-communication-efficie.tldr: LESS-VFL uses server guidance followed by local feature selection to remove spurious features with substantially less communication.

paragraphs: Machine learning force fields can accelerate molecular dynamics, but producing accurate energy and force labels can be expensive. Even data-efficient models may need hundreds of labeled molecular configurations generated by quantum mechanical calculations. ASTEROID addresses this data-generation cost by combining a large quantity of inexpensive, inaccurate data with a small quantity of accurate data.

The method first trains a force-field model on the cheaper data. Its motivation is that biased measurements can still reveal complicated structure in the underlying force field. A bias-aware loss discourages the model from overfitting the inexpensive data's systematic errors. Fine-tuning on accurate data then improves precision while preserving knowledge acquired during the first stage.

The authors also introduce a score-matching variant for situations where the inexpensive data lack labels. Experiments on molecular dynamics datasets and downstream tasks support the framework's effectiveness. The contribution makes training sensitive to the cost and quality of its data sources, using expensive supervision to refine a model that has already learned from cheaper information.
icml-2023-machine-learning-force-fields-.tldr: ASTEROID lowers force-field training data costs by learning from cheap, biased data before fine-tuning on a small accurate dataset.

paragraphs: Inferring an agent's reward function from its behavior is often studied using demonstrations from an expert or an agent already near optimal performance. Learning from a Learner instead uses demonstrations produced as a policy improves. This paper extends that perspective to interacting agents whose behavior changes during learning in a general-sum stochastic game.

The proposed MA-LfL algorithm aims to recover the agents' reward functions without assuming that their demonstrations come from an equilibrium. This distinction matters because ongoing adaptation is part of the observed process. The method treats a sequence of improving policies as evidence about what the agents are trying to achieve.

A theoretical result establishes the algorithm's validity when the agents learn through a multi-agent soft policy iteration scheme. The guarantee is therefore tied to a particular learning process, even though equilibrium is not required. Empirical tests show high positive correlation between recovered rewards and ground truth, supporting the approach's ability to infer reward structure in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-multi-agent-learning-from-lear.tldr: MA-LfL infers rewards from interacting agents still learning, with theoretical validity under multi-agent soft policy iteration.

paragraphs: Dexterous hand control requires coordinating many joints and muscles during contact with objects. This paper takes inspiration from the way diverse prior experience supports human skill acquisition. Its goal is to develop agents that can reuse experience across manipulation tasks and acquire new behaviors more quickly, including behaviors that were previously unattainable.

The authors train across multiple tasks using MyoHand, a physiologically realistic human hand model. This process implicitly develops MyoDex, a behavioral prior intended to be useful beyond any individual training task. The central idea is that experience with varied manipulation behaviors can provide a shared foundation for learning additional forms of physiological control.

The reported results demonstrate few-shot generalization and positive transfer across a large collection of unseen manipulation tasks. Compared with a distillation baseline, MyoDex solves approximately three times as many tasks and reaches solutions about four times faster. These comparisons support the value of the learned prior in the evaluated setting, especially for transferring experience across diverse contact-rich behaviors.
icml-2023-myodex-a-generalizable-prior-f.tldr: MyoDex learns reusable hand-control experience across tasks, improving transfer and learning speed for unseen dexterous manipulation behaviors.

paragraphs: Graph Transformers and message-passing neural networks are often treated as distinct approaches to graph learning. Earlier theory showed that suitably equipped Transformers can approximate message-passing networks. This paper studies the reverse direction, showing that adding a virtual node gives a message-passing network enough expressive power to approximate Transformer self-attention.

The required network size depends on the attention mechanism and construction. A Performer or Linear Transformer attention layer can be approximated with constant depth and width. For general self-attention, one construction uses constant depth and width growing as O(n^d), where d is the feature dimension. Another, under additional assumptions, uses constant width and depth growing as O(n).

Experiments also establish the virtual-node model as a strong practical baseline. It outperforms Graph Transformers on the reported Long Range Graph Benchmark evaluation, improves on an earlier implementation across OGB datasets, and beats Linear Transformer and ordinary message passing on a climate task. The findings connect representational capability with empirical competitiveness while preserving the differing resource requirements of the theoretical constructions.
icml-2023-on-the-connection-between-mpnn.tldr: Message-passing networks with a virtual node can approximate Transformer attention and perform strongly in the reported graph-learning experiments.

paragraphs: Text models typically begin by converting tokens into numerical vectors. Understanding how those vectors change when words are replaced is a discrete robustness problem, which differs from studying small changes to continuous numerical inputs. This paper analyzes that initial conversion step for several widely used ways of representing text.

The authors prove Hölder or Lipschitz robustness for concatenation, TF-IDF, and Paragraph Vector, also known as doc2vec, with respect to Hamming distance. In this formulation, changes in a text representation are bounded in relation to the number of differing token positions. The guarantees make the relationship between discrete input changes and numerical representation changes mathematically explicit.

The paper supplies quantitative bounds and examines how document length affects their constants. This matters because a robustness statement becomes more informative when its sensitivity to input length is understood. Numerical examples illustrate the findings. The results concern the stability of the vectorization schemes themselves, providing a precise characterization of an early stage through which text enters a learning model.
icml-2023-on-the-robustness-of-text-vect.tldr: The paper proves quantitative robustness bounds for common text vectorizers under token changes and characterizes their dependence on document length.

paragraphs: When a low-rank matrix has very few observed entries, recovering every missing value may be impossible. This paper asks whether useful structure can still be recovered. It studies one-sided matrix completion: estimating the right singular vectors even in a regime where the left singular vectors cannot be recovered.

The setting has more rows than columns and very sparse observations within each row. The proposed algorithm works by filling missing values in XᵀX, which captures relationships between the columns. This changes the recovery target from the original matrix to an object that can preserve the desired one-sided structure despite insufficient information for full completion.

The authors prove recovery of XᵀX with only two observations per row when the number of rows is at least on the order of r²d log d, with rank r and d columns. Experiments on synthetic data and low-coverage genome sequencing show substantial advantages over standard matrix completion and several direct factorization methods. The results demonstrate the value of targeting recoverable structure in extremely sparse data.
icml-2023-one-sided-matrix-completion-fr.tldr: One-sided matrix completion recovers column-side structure from two observations per row when sufficiently many rows are available.

paragraphs: A receiver choosing an action may depend on information supplied by strategic senders. Those senders observe the underlying state but may report it dishonestly. This paper designs information-acquisition mechanisms that maximize the receiver's utility while making truthful reporting incentive compatible. It first gives an efficient algorithm for computing an optimal mechanism.

The authors then consider repeated interactions in an unknown game. Here the receiver must learn while controlling both cumulative regret relative to the optimal incentive-compatible mechanism and cumulative violations of truthfulness constraints. Tracking both quantities makes explicit that good decisions and good incentives are separate objectives during learning.

With full feedback, the proposed algorithm bounds both quantities at approximately √T, up to logarithmic factors. With bandit feedback, it offers regret of approximately T^α and violation of approximately T^(1−α/2), for α between one-half and one. This exposes a tradeoff between the two guarantees under limited feedback. A tight lower bound complements the algorithms and characterizes a limit on achievable performance.
icml-2023-online-mechanism-design-for-in.tldr: The paper develops information-acquisition mechanisms that jointly control decision regret and truthfulness-constraint violations while learning an unknown game.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether robustness to image corruptions can be extracted from model weights and transferred through simple arithmetic. Comparing models with the same architecture trained on clean and corrupted data, the authors observe that most weight differences occur in shallow layers. A projected version of this difference becomes a Robust Weight Signature, or RWS.

The signatures empirically distinguish corruption types and, for a fixed architecture and corruption type, transfer consistently across datasets. The proposed framework stores a clean model alongside extracted signatures. Adding a signature patches its weights, removing it restores the clean model, and rescaling it adjusts the strength of the robustness patch.

Experiments also support combining several signatures and retaining useful patches as the clean backbone is adapted or updated. Concentration in shallow layers and quantization make a signature up to 13 times smaller than a full weight copy. These are empirical findings about the evaluated patches, suggesting that some learned robustness can be stored and manipulated as compact, transferable weight differences.
icml-2023-robust-weight-signatures-gaini.tldr: Empirical results suggest corruption robustness can be transferred, adjusted, and combined through compact additive patches to model weights.

paragraphs: Safe policy improvement seeks to improve a reinforcement learning policy while retaining a safety relationship to a baseline. This paper develops MCTS-SPIBB, which applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to compute such improvements online. Its purpose is to make the SPIBB approach usable in larger problems by concentrating computation where the agent needs decisions.

The key change is local planning. MCTS-SPIBB computes policy decisions in states the agent actually visits, using simulations to guide the search. This differs operationally from the policy-iteration approach underlying SPIBB and reduces the need to compute a policy across a much larger collection of states.

The authors prove that, as the number of simulations grows, the generated policy converges to the optimal safely improved policy produced by SPIBB. This is a convergence statement about increasing search effort. Experiments on three standard benchmark domains show that the method scales to significantly larger problems than SPIBB, supporting online, local computation as a practical route to scaling the same safe-improvement objective.
icml-2023-scalable-safe-policy-improveme.tldr: MCTS-SPIBB scales safe policy improvement through local online search that converges to SPIBB's optimal safely improved policy as simulations increase.

paragraphs: Skeleton-based action recognition represents human movement through joints and their relationships. Ske2Grid learns to arrange this information into a compact, image-like grid so that regular convolution can operate on it. The paper's contribution is a coordinated set of transformations for constructing and progressively learning that grid representation.

A graph-node index transform assigns skeleton nodes to grid cells. A learned upsampling transform interpolates additional nodes to fill the grid, supporting a one-to-one assignment and a more expressive representation. Because a large expansion in a single step can be too aggressive, the method breaks upsampling into several stages paired with corresponding index transforms.

These stages form a compact cascade trained progressively as the grid grows. The authors build networks on established graph convolution architectures and evaluate them on six mainstream skeleton-based action recognition datasets. They report significant improvements over existing graph convolution solutions across benchmark settings. The findings support learning how skeleton information is arranged for convolution as a useful component of action-recognition modeling.
icml-2023-ske2grid-skeleton-to-grid-repr.tldr: Ske2Grid progressively maps skeleton graphs into learned image-like grids, improving action recognition in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Learning nonlinear state-space models requires reasoning about hidden states from observed sequences. For maximum likelihood estimation and Markov Score Climbing, an important step is estimating smoothing expectations of additive quantities. Errors in these estimates matter because both bias and variance affect the convergence analysis of the learning procedure.

The paper introduces the Parisian particle Gibbs sampler, or PPG, as a new additive smoothing algorithm. It combines the PaRIS approach with conditional sequential Monte Carlo moves to produce estimates with reduced bias. The authors develop bounds on bias and variance, together with deviation inequalities that characterize estimation errors.

They then analyze PPG within learning algorithms and establish finite-computation bounds under standard assumptions. These results highlight benefits from bias reduction and the sampler's implicit Rao–Blackwellization, an averaging effect that improves estimation. Numerical experiments support the theoretical claims. The contribution links the design of a better smoothing estimator to explicit guarantees for learning states and parameters from sequential observations.
icml-2023-state-and-parameter-learning-w.tldr: Parisian particle Gibbs reduces smoothing-estimation bias and supports finite-computation learning guarantees for nonlinear state-space models.

paragraphs: Multi-goal reinforcement learning allows an agent to reuse experience across related tasks. Exploration becomes difficult, however, when rewards are sparse and discontinuities in the goal space leave many goals hard to reach. A curriculum can help by selecting training goals that fit the agent's current capabilities rather than presenting mostly unattainable tasks.

Stein Variational Goal Generation, or SVGG, learns a predictive model of the agent's ability to reach goals. It uses that model to identify goals of intermediate difficulty. A collection of particles represents the goal distribution, and Stein Variational Gradient Descent moves those particles toward regions with an appropriate level of challenge.

The curriculum thus adapts its goal distribution using estimates of what the agent can currently accomplish. Experiments show higher success coverage than state-of-the-art multi-goal reinforcement learning methods on the evaluated hard-exploration problems. The authors also demonstrate useful recovery when the environment changes. These findings support adaptive goal generation as a way to improve exploration and respond to changed task conditions.
icml-2023-stein-variational-goal-generat.tldr: SVGG adapts a particle-based goal curriculum to the agent's capabilities, improving success coverage and demonstrating recovery after environmental changes.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning builds representations from raw data without supervision, but its training behavior can be difficult to manage. Optimizer tuning may be unstable, and representations can collapse during training. This paper treats those challenges as motivation for understanding how data augmentation, network architecture, and the training algorithm interact.

The authors study that interaction in kernel regimes, where they carry out a precise analysis of generalization. Their analysis covers both the pretraining task and downstream tasks. Considering both stages matters because learning a representation and using that representation for another task are distinct parts of the self-supervised learning process.

The contribution is a theoretical account connecting these design choices to generalization performance, along with practitioner insights arising from that account. Its stated scope is the kernel setting, which supplies the framework for the analysis. The abstract does not enumerate the individual insights; its central message is that augmentation, architectural bias, and training dynamics should be understood together when analyzing self-supervised representations.
icml-2023-the-ssl-interplay-augmentation.tldr: The paper analyzes how augmentations, architecture, and training interact to shape self-supervised generalization in kernel regimes.

paragraphs: Latent Gaussian process inference needs approximations that balance computational cost with accuracy. This paper proposes a variational family of Gaussian distributions whose covariance matrices have sparse inverse Cholesky factors. The sparse factor structure provides a way to restrict the computation while still representing dependencies within the Gaussian distribution.

The method approximates both the posterior and the prior using related sparse structures and Kullback–Leibler objectives. This pairing gives the approach its name, double-Kullback–Leibler-optimal Gaussian-process approximation, or DKLGP. The authors focus on a particular ordering and nearest-neighbor sparsity pattern that produce highly accurate approximations of both distributions.

For this particular setting, stochastic gradient descent can compute the variational approximation with polylogarithmic time per iteration. Numerical comparisons show that, with stationary kernels, DKLGP can sometimes be vastly more accurate than inducing-point or mean-field alternatives at similar computational complexity. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is possible and empirically demonstrated, while the efficient computation result depends on the selected sparse construction.
icml-2023-variational-sparse-inverse-cho.tldr: DKLGP sparsely approximates both Gaussian-process prior and posterior, sometimes delivering much higher accuracy at comparable computational cost.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks are often said to succeed because they match the local, hierarchical structure of data. This paper asks how that structure quantitatively affects learning as more training samples become available. It studies infinitely wide, deep convolutional networks in the kernel regime and characterizes the spectrum of their associated kernel.

The authors show that this spectrum reflects the network's hierarchy. Combining that characterization with generalization bounds, they establish that learning adapts to the target function's spatial scale. When the target depends on low-dimensional groups of adjacent inputs, error decay is governed by those groups' effective dimensionality. When it depends on all inputs, the full input dimension controls the decay.

The paper also computes generalization error when one deep convolutional network learns outputs generated by another with randomly initialized parameters. In this infinite-width setting, the generated functions remain too rich to learn efficiently in high dimensions. The findings clarify that hierarchical architecture alone does not ensure efficient learning; the target's particular dependence on the inputs matters.
icml-2023-what-can-be-learnt-with-wide-c.tldr: Infinite-width convolutional networks benefit from local low-dimensional targets, but hierarchical structure alone does not ensure efficient high-dimensional learning.
